entries.4d35493e954f7e479b25f580c21e56aa7589cb37: <div sID="gen7803" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="1Chr.16" sID="1Chr.16"/> <div eID="gen7803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7804" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7805" type="x-p"/> This chapter concludes that great affair of the settlement of the ark in the royal city, and with it the settlement of the public worship of God during the reign of David. Here is, I. The solemnity with which the ark was fixed, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.1-1Chr.16.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. The psalm David gave to be sung on this occasion, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.7-1Chr.16.36">ver. 7-36</reference>. III. The settling of the stated public worship of God in order thenceforward, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.37-1Chr.16.43">ver. 37-43</reference>.
entries.65707b24dd5f4a0dc13c84be409ae2d1bb525188: <div eID="gen7805" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7804" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Settlement of the Ark. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1045.)</title> <div sID="gen7806" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> So they brought the ark of God, and set it in the midst of the tent that David had pitched for it: and they offered burnt sacrifices and peace offerings before God. <hi type="super">2</hi> And when David had made an end of offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">3</hi> And he dealt to every one of Israel, both man and woman, to every one a loaf of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon <hi type="italic">of wine.</hi> <hi type="super">4</hi> And he appointed <hi type="italic">certain</hi> of the Levites to minister before the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and to record, and to thank and praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel: <hi type="super">5</hi> Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah, Jeiel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Mattithiah, and Eliab, and Benaiah, and Obed-edom: and Jeiel with psalteries and with harps; but Asaph made a sound with cymbals; <hi type="super">6</hi> Benaiah also and Jahaziel the priests with trumpets continually before the ark of the covenant of God. <div eID="gen7806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7807" type="x-p"/> It was a glorious day when the ark of God was safely lodged in the tent David had pitched for it. That good man had his heart much upon it, could not sleep contentedly till it was done, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.4-Ps.132.5">Ps. cxxxii. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen7807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7808" type="x-p"/> I. The circumstances of the ark were now, 1. Better than what they had been. It had been obscure in a country town, in the fields of the wood; now it was removed to a public place, to the royal city, where all might resort to it. It had been neglected, as a despised broken vessel; now it was attended with veneration, and God was enquired of by it. It had borrowed a room in a private house, which it enjoyed by courtesy; now it had a habitation of its own entirely to itself, was set in the midst of it, and not crowded into a corner. Note, Though God's word and ordinances may be clouded and eclipsed for a time, they shall at length shine out of obscurity. Yet, 2. They were much short of what was intended in the next reign, when the temple was to be built. This was but a tent, a poor mean dwelling; yet this was the tabernacle, the temple which David in his psalms often speaks of with so much affection. David, who pitched a tent for the ark and continued steadfast to it, did far better than Solomon, who built a temple for it and yet in his latter end turned his back upon it. The church's poorest times were its purest. <div eID="gen7808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7809" type="x-p"/> II. Now David was easy in his mind, the ark was fixed, and fixed near him. Now see how he takes care, 1. That God shall have the glory of it. Two ways he gives him honour upon this occasion:—(1.) By sacrifices (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.1">v. 1</reference>), burnt-offerings in adoration of his perfections, peace-offerings in acknowledgment of his favours. (2.) By songs: he appointed Levites to record this story in a song for the benefit of others, or to celebrate it themselves by <hi type="italic">thanking and praising the God of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.4">v. 4</reference>. All our rejoicings must express themselves in thanksgivings to him from whom all our comforts are received. 2. That the people shall have the joy of it. They shall fare the better for this day's solemnity; for he gives them all what is worth coming for, not only a royal treat in honour of the day (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.3">v. 3</reference>), in which David showed himself generous to his subjects, as he had found God gracious to him (those whose hearts are enlarged with holy joy should show it by being open-handed); but (which is far better) he gives them also a <hi type="italic">blessing in the name of the Lord,</hi> as a father, as a prophet, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.2">v. 2</reference>. He prayed to God for them, and commended them to his grace. <hi type="italic">In the name of the Word of the Lord</hi> (so the Targum), the essential eternal Word, who is Jehovah, and through whom all blessings come to us.
entries.78883c2b514d3fa695a71dd73533648b0f9c5f85: <div eID="gen7809" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Psalm of Praise. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1045.)</title> <div sID="gen7810" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Then on that day David delivered first <hi type="italic">this psalm</hi> to thank the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> into the hand of Asaph and his brethren. <hi type="super">8</hi> Give thanks unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , call upon his name, make known his deeds among the people. <hi type="super">9</hi> Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works. <hi type="super">10</hi> Glory ye in his holy name: let the heart of them rejoice that seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">11</hi> Seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> and his strength, seek his face continually. <hi type="super">12</hi> Remember his marvellous works that he hath done, his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth; <hi type="super">13</hi> O ye seed of Israel his servant, ye children of Jacob, his chosen ones. <hi type="super">14</hi> He <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God; his judgments <hi type="italic">are</hi> in all the earth. <hi type="super">15</hi> Be ye mindful always of his covenant; the word <hi type="italic">which</hi> he commanded to a thousand generations; <hi type="super">16</hi> <hi type="italic">Even of the covenant</hi> which he made with Abraham, and of his oath unto Isaac; <hi type="super">17</hi> And hath confirmed the same to Jacob for a law, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to Israel <hi type="italic">for</hi> an everlasting covenant, <hi type="super">18</hi> Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance; <hi type="super">19</hi> When ye were but few, even a few, and strangers in it. <hi type="super">20</hi> And <hi type="italic">when</hi> they went from nation to nation, and from <hi type="italic">one</hi> kingdom to another people; <hi type="super">21</hi> He suffered no man to do them wrong: yea, he reproved kings for their sakes,   22 <hi type="italic">Saying,</hi> Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm. <hi type="super">23</hi> Sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all the earth; shew forth from day to day his salvation. <hi type="super">24</hi> Declare his glory among the heathen; his marvellous works among all nations. <hi type="super">25</hi> For great <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and greatly to be praised: he also <hi type="italic">is</hi> to be feared above all gods. <hi type="super">26</hi> For all the gods of the people <hi type="italic">are</hi> idols: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> made the heavens. <hi type="super">27</hi> Glory and honour <hi type="italic">are</hi> in his presence; strength and gladness <hi type="italic">are</hi> in his place. <hi type="super">28</hi> Give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , ye kindreds of the people, give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> glory and strength. <hi type="super">29</hi> Give unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the glory <hi type="italic">due</hi> unto his name: bring an offering, and come before him: worship the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the beauty of holiness. <hi type="super">30</hi> Fear before him, all the earth: the world also shall be stable, that it be not moved. <hi type="super">31</hi> Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice: and let <hi type="italic">men</hi> say among the nations, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> reigneth. <hi type="super">32</hi> Let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof: let the fields rejoice, and all that <hi type="italic">is</hi> therein. <hi type="super">33</hi> Then shall the trees of the wood sing out at the presence of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because he cometh to judge the earth. <hi type="super">34</hi> O give thanks unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for <hi type="italic">he is</hi> good; for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">35</hi> And say ye, Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather us together, and deliver us from the heathen, that we may give thanks to thy holy name, <hi type="italic">and</hi> glory in thy praise. <hi type="super">36</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel for ever and ever. And all the people said, Amen, and praised the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen7810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7811" type="x-p"/> We have here the thanksgiving psalm which David, by the Spirit, composed, and delivered to the chief musician, to be sung upon occasion of the public entry the ark made into the tent prepared for it. Some think he appointed this hymn to be daily used in the temple service, as duly as the day came; whatever other psalms they sung, they must not omit this. David had penned many psalms before this, some in the time of his trouble by Saul. This was composed before, but was now first delivered into the hand of Asaph, for the use of the church. It is gathered out of several psalms (from the <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.7-1Chr.16.23">beginning to v. 23</reference> is taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.105.1-Ps.105.15">Ps. cv. 1</reference>, &c.; and then <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23-1Chr.16.34">v. 23 to v. 34</reference> is the whole <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">96th psalm</reference>, with little variation; <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34">v. 34</reference> is taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.136.1">Ps. cxxxvi. 1</reference> and divers others; and then the <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.35-1Chr.16.36">last two verses</reference> are taken from the close of <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47-Ps.106.48">Ps. cvi.</reference>), which some think warrants us to do likewise, and make up hymns out of David's psalms, a part of one and a part of another put together so as may be most proper to express and excite the devotion of Christians. These psalms will be best expounded in their proper places (if the Lord will); here we take them as they are put together, with a design to <hi type="italic">thank the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.7">v. 7</reference>), a great duty, to which we need to be excited and in which we need to be assisted. 1. Let God be glorified in our praises; let his honour be the centre in which all the lines meet. Let us glorify him by our thanksgivings (<hi type="italic">Give thanks to the Lord</hi>), by our prayers (<hi type="italic">Call on his name,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8">v. 8</reference>), by our songs <hi type="italic">(Sing psalms unto him</hi>), by our discourse—<hi type="italic">Talk of all his wondrous works,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.9">v. 9</reference>. Let us glorify him as <hi type="italic">a great God, and greatly to be praised</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.25">v. 25</reference>), as supreme God (above all gods), as sole God, for all others are idols, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.26">v. 26</reference>. Let us glorify him as most bright and blessed in himself (<hi type="italic">Glory and honour are in his presence,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.27">v. 27</reference>), as creator (<hi type="italic">The Lord made the heavens</hi>), as the ruler of the whole creation (<hi type="italic">His judgments are in all the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.14">v. 14</reference>), and as ours—<hi type="italic">He is the Lord our God.</hi> Thus must we <hi type="italic">give unto the Lord the glory due to his name</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.28-1Chr.16.29">v. 28, 29</reference>), and own it, and much more, his due. 2. Let other be edified and instructed: <hi type="italic">Make known his deeds among the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">declare his glory among the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.24">v. 24</reference>), that those who are strangers to him may be led into acquaintance with him, allegiance to him, and the adoration of him. Thus must we serve the interests of his kingdom among men, that all the earth may <hi type="italic">fear before him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.30">v. 30</reference>. 3. Let us be ourselves encouraged to triumph and trust in God. Those that give glory to God's name are allowed to <hi type="italic">glory in it</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.10">v. 10</reference>), to value themselves upon their relation to God and venture themselves upon his promise to them. <hi type="italic">Let the heart of those rejoice that seek the Lord,</hi> much more of those that have found him. <hi type="italic">Seek him, and his strength, and his face:</hi> that is, seek him by the ark of his strength, in which he manifests himself. 4. Let the everlasting covenant be the great matter of our joy and praise (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be mindful of his covenant.</hi> In the parallel place it is, <hi type="italic">He will be ever mindful of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.8">Ps. cv. 8</reference>. Seeing God never will forget it, we never must. The covenant is said to be <hi type="italic">commanded,</hi> because God has obliged us to obey the conditions of it, and because he has both authority to make the promise and ability to make it good. This covenant was ancient, yet never to be forgotten. It was made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who were long since dead (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.16-1Chr.16.18">v. 16-18</reference>), yet still sure to the spiritual seed, and the promises of it pleadable. 5. Let God's former mercies to his people of old, to our ancestors and our predecessors in profession, be commemorated by us now with thankfulness to his praise. Let it be remembered how God protected the patriarchs in their unsettled condition. When they came strangers to Canaan and were sojourners in it, when they were few and might easily have been swallowed up, when they were continually upon the remove and so exposed, when there were many that bore them ill-will and sought to do them mischief, yet no man was suffered to do them wrong—not the Canaanites, Philistines, Egyptians. Kings were reproved and plagued for their sakes. Pharaoh was so, and Abimelech. They were the <hi type="italic">anointed of the Lord,</hi> sanctified by his grace, sanctified by his glory, and had received the unction of the Spirit. They were his prophets, instructed in the things of God themselves and commissioned to instruct others (and prophets are said to be <hi type="italic">anointed,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.16">1 Kings xix. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>); therefore, if any touch them, they touch the apple of God's eye; if any harm them, it is at their peril, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.19-1Chr.16.22">v. 19-22</reference>. 6. Let the great salvation of the Lord be especially the subject of our praises (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Show forth from day to day his salvation,</hi> that is (says bishop Patrick), his promised salvation by Christ. We have reason to celebrate that from day to day; for we daily receive the benefits of it, and it is a subject that can never be exhausted. 7. Let God be praised by a due and constant attendance upon him in the ordinances he has appointed: <hi type="italic">Bring an offering,</hi> then the fruit of the <hi type="italic">ground,</hi> now the fruit of the <hi type="italic">lips,</hi> of the <hi type="italic">heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>), and <hi type="italic">worship him in the beauty of holiness,</hi> in the holy places and in a holy manner, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.29">v. 29</reference>. Holiness is the beauty of the Lord, the beauty of all sanctified souls and all religious performances. 8. Let God's universal monarchy be the fear and joy of all people. Let us reverence it: <hi type="italic">Fear before him, all the earth.</hi> And let us rejoice in it: <hi type="italic">Let the heavens be glad and rejoice,</hi> because <hi type="italic">the Lord reigns,</hi> and by his providence establishes the world, so that, though it be moved, it cannot be removed, nor the measures broken which Infinite Wisdom has taken in the government of it, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.30-1Chr.16.31">v. 30, 31</reference>. 9. Let the prospect of the judgment to come inspire us with an awful pleasure, Let earth and sea, fields and woods, though in the great day of the Lord they will all be consumed, yet rejoice that he will come, doth come, to <hi type="italic">judge the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.32-1Chr.16.33">v. 32, 33</reference>. 10. In the midst of our praises we must not forget to pray for the succour and relief of those saints and servants of God that are in distress (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">Save us, gather us, deliver us from the heathen,</hi> those of us that are scattered and oppressed. When we are rejoicing in God's favours to us we must remember our afflicted brethren, and pray for their salvation and deliverance as our own. We are members one of another; and therefore when we mean, "Lord, save <hi type="italic">them,</hi>" it is not improper to say, "Lord, save <hi type="italic">us.</hi>" <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Let us make God the Alpha and Omega of our praises. David begins with (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Give thanks to the Lord;</hi> he concludes (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.36">v. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord.</hi> And whereas in the place whence this doxology is taken (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Ps. cvi. 48</reference>) it is added, <hi type="italic">Let all the people say, Amen, Hallelujah,</hi> here we find they did according to that directory: <hi type="italic">All the people said, Amen, and praised the Lord.</hi> When the Levites had finished this psalm or prayer and praise, then, and not till then, the people that attended signified their consent and concurrence by saying, <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> And so they praised the Lord, much affected no doubt with this newly instituted way of devotion, which had been hitherto used in the schools of the prophets only, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1 Sam. x. 5</reference>. And, if this way of praising God <hi type="italic">please the Lord better than an ox or a bullock that has horns and hoofs, the humble shall see it and be glad,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.31-Ps.69.32">Ps. lxix. 31, 32</reference>.
entries.d57933eabcce1b2c40e47bec216cee2baf9ea6e2: <div eID="gen7811" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Service of the Ark. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1045.)</title> <div sID="gen7812" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">37</hi> So he left there before the ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> Asaph and his brethren, to minister before the ark continually, as every day's work required: <hi type="super">38</hi> And Obed-edom with their brethren, threescore and eight; Obed-edom also the son of Jeduthun and Hosah <hi type="italic">to be</hi> porters: <hi type="super">39</hi> And Zadok the priest, and his brethren the priests, before the tabernacle of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the high place that <hi type="italic">was</hi> at Gibeon, <hi type="super">40</hi> To offer burnt offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> upon the altar of the burnt offering continually morning and evening, and <hi type="italic">to do</hi> according to all that is written in the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which he commanded Israel; <hi type="super">41</hi> And with them Heman and Jeduthun, and the rest that were chosen, who were expressed by name, to give thanks to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever; <hi type="super">42</hi> And with them Heman and Jeduthun with trumpets and cymbals for those that should make a sound, and with musical instruments of God. And the sons of Jeduthun <hi type="italic">were</hi> porters. <hi type="super">43</hi> And all the people departed every man to his house: and David returned to bless his house. <div eID="gen7812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7813" type="x-p"/> The worship of God is not only to be the work of a solemn day now and then, brought in to grace a triumph; but it ought to be the work of every day. David therefore settles it here for a constancy, puts it into a method, which he obliged those that officiated to observe in their respective posts. In the tabernacle of Moses, and afterwards in the temple of Solomon, the ark and the altar were together; but, ever since Eli's time, they had been separated, and still continued so till the temple was built. I cannot conceive what reason there was why David, who knew the law and was zealous for it, did not either bring the ark to Gibeon, where the tabernacle and the altar were, or bring them to Mount Zion, where the ark was. Perhaps the curtains and hangings of Moses's tabernacle were so worn with time and weather that they were not fit to be removed, nor fit to be a shelter for the ark; and yet he would not make all new, but only a tent for the ark, because the time was at hand when the temple should be built. Whatever was the reason, all David's time they were asunder, but he took care that neither of them should be neglected. 1. At Jerusalem, where the ark was, Asaph and his brethren were appointed to attend, to <hi type="italic">minister before the ark continually,</hi> with songs of praise, <hi type="italic">as every day's work required,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.37">v. 37</reference>. No sacrifices were offered there, nor incense burnt, because the altars were not there: but David's prayers were <hi type="italic">directed as incense, and the lifting up of his hands as the evening sacrifice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Ps. cxli. 2</reference>), so early did spiritual worship take place of ceremonial. 2. Yet the ceremonial worship, being of divine institution, must by no means be omitted; and therefore at Gibeon were the altars where the priests attended, for their work was to sacrifice and burn incense, which they did <hi type="italic">continually, morning and evening, according to the law of Moses,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39-1Chr.16.40">v. 39, 40</reference>. These must be kept up because, however in their own nature they were inferior to the moral services of prayer and praise, yet, as they were types of the mediation of Christ, they had a great deal of honour put upon them, and the observance of them was of great consequence. Here Zadok attended, to preside in the service of the altar; as (it is probable) Abiathar settled at Jerusalem, to attend the ark, because he had the breast-plate of judgment, which must be consulted before the ark: this is the reason why we read in David's time both Zadok and Abiathar were the priests (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.17">2 Sam. viii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.25">xx. 25</reference>), one where the altar was and the other where the ark was. At Gibeon, where the altars were, David also appointed <hi type="italic">singers to give thanks to the Lord,</hi> and the burden of all their songs must be, <hi type="italic">For his mercy endureth for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.41">v. 41</reference>. They did it <hi type="italic">with musical instruments of God,</hi> such instruments as were appointed and appropriated to this service, not such as they used on other occasions. Between common mirth and holy joy there is a vast difference, and the limits and distances between them must be carefully observed and kept up. Matters being thus settled, and the affairs of religion put into a happy channel, (1.) The people were satisfied, and went home pleased. (2.) David returned to bless his house, resolving to keep up family worship still, which public worship must not supersede.  <chapter eID="1Chr.16"/> <div eID="gen7813" type="x-p"/>

entries.41e555d2e9d2d0447f2d150d5399dbef35f3d923: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3782"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <div sID="gen5422" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.1-1Chr.16.6">1Ch 16:1-6</reference>. David's Festival Sacrifice and Liberality to the People.<div eID="gen5422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5423" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3782"/><hi type="bold">2. he blessed the people in the name of the Lord--</hi>The king commended their zeal, supplicated the divine blessing upon them, and ordered the remains of the thank offerings which had been profusely sacrificed during the procession, to be distributed in certain proportions to every individual, that the ceremonial might terminate with appropriate festivities (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.7">De 12:7</reference>). <div eID="gen5423" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b66c29724523afcf89de95d7c151a4bce057937: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3783"/><div sID="gen5424" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3783"/><hi type="bold">3. flagon of wine--</hi>The two latter words are a supplement by our translators, and the former is, in other versions, rendered not a "flagon," but a "cake," a confection, as the Septuagint renders it, made of flour and honey. <div eID="gen5424" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9c89f0c0b01a595c93387cdc270efa36b52c272: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3784"/><div sID="gen5425" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3784"/><hi type="bold">4-6. he appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of the Lord--</hi>No sooner was the ark deposited in its tent than the Levites, who were to officiate in the choirs before it, entered upon their duties. A select number of the musicians were chosen for the service from the list (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19-1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:19-21</reference>) of those who had taken a prominent part in the recent procession. The same arrangement was to be observed in their duties, now that the ark again was stationary; Asaph, with his associates, composing the first or principal company, played with cymbals; Zechariah and his colleagues, with whom were conjoined Jeiel and Obed-edom, forming the second company, used harps and similar instruments. <div eID="gen5425" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f2795cc4d88e1117c23edd83bd8395aa23c91c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3787"/><div sID="gen5429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3787"/><hi type="bold">7. Then on that day David delivered first this psalm--</hi>Among the other preparations for this solemn inauguration, the royal bard had composed a special hymn for the occasion. Doubtless it had been previously in the hands of Asaph and his assistants, but it was now publicly committed to them as they entered for the first time on the performance of their sacred duties. It occupies the greater part of this chapter (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:8-36</reference>), and seems to have been compiled from other psalms of David, previously known to the Israelites, as the whole of it will be found, with very slight variations, in Psa 96:1-13; 105:1-15; 106:47,48. In the form, however, in which it is given by the sacred historian, it seems to have been the first psalm given for use in the tabernacle service. Abounding, as it does, with the liveliest ascriptions of praise to God for the revelation of His glorious character and the display of His marvellous works and containing, as it does, so many pointed allusions to the origin, privileges, and peculiar destiny of the chosen people, it was admirably calculated to animate the devotions and call forth the gratitude of the assembled multitude. <div eID="gen5429" type="x-p"/>
entries.dddebea1a2a12b77e28b50f831f1c9615e45eafd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3788"/><div sID="gen5430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3788"/><hi type="bold">36. all the people said, Amen--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.72.19">Psa 72:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">106:48</reference>). In the former, the author of the doxology utters the "amen" himself, while in the latter the people are exhorted to say "amen." This may arise from the fact that the latter psalm originally concluded with the injunction to say "amen." But in this historical account of the festival, it was necessary to relate that the people obeyed this injunction on the occasion referred to, and therefore the words "let them praise," were altered into "and they praised" [Bertheau]. <div eID="gen5430" type="x-p"/>
entries.a68d0fabfa712a2e1b7ea1dde6a44a785ebfaa05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3789"/><div sID="gen5431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3789"/><hi type="bold">37-42. So he left there before the ark of the covenant of the Lord Asaph and his brethren, &c.--</hi>The sequel of the chapter describes the appointment of the sacred musicians and their respective duties. <div eID="gen5431" type="x-p"/>

entries.f76f8efa27f35a12af4cab4e207ebe2a86867c57: <div eID="gen13644" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13645" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13646" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13646" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13645" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13647" type="x-p"/> David brings the ark into its tent; and offers sacrifices, peace-offerings, and burnt-offerings, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.1">1Chr 16:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.2">1Chr 16:2</reference>; and gives portions to the people of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.3">1Chr 16:3</reference>. He appoints proper ministers and officers for the ark, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.4-1Chr.16.6">1Chr 16:4-6</reference>. He delivers a solemn thanksgiving on the occasion, vv. 7-36. How the different officers served at the ark, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.37-1Chr.16.42">1Chr 16:37-42</reference>. The people return home, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.43">1Chr 16:43</reference>.
entries.f5b32ef0a3301977c0ee6c579f3c4cac53bec84a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13648" type="x-p"/> He blessed the people - "He blessed the people in the name of the Word of the Lord." - T.
entries.396658b6c90127fd0201bd7264db6928fb7f5300: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen13648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13649" type="x-p"/> To every one a loaf of bread - A whole cake. A good piece of flesh; "the sixth part of an ox, and the sixth part of a hin of wine." - T. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.18-2Sam.6.20">2Sam 6:18-20</reference>; see Jarchi also.
entries.1ef7fc3b39818c4c6eb809b888da4983767ff00e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen13649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13650" type="x-p"/> Asaph - See the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.17">1Chr 15:17</reference> (note), etc.
entries.629ac9a4e50ad1b2097e9fdf956f0ccd80c67951: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen13650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13651" type="x-p"/> David delivered first this psalm - I believe the meaning of this place to be this: David made the psalm on the occasion above specified; and delivered it to Asaph, who was the musician, and to his brethren, to be sung by them in honor of what God had done in behalf of his people.
entries.2370d8c37cb9d907d488ab3f51ad1d7a1e5c9f38: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen13651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13652" type="x-p"/> That seek the Lord - "That seek the Word of the Lord." - T.
entries.d747c8eb1796ff7cf4b62595767bb183947f2246: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen13652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13653" type="x-p"/> Remember his marvellous works - The whole of the psalm refers to God's wondrous actions among the nations in behalf of Israel.
entries.57c9edbbafaa594c00d73f2fa15bb5b2f205786d: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen13653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13654" type="x-p"/> Touch not mine anointed - By this title the patriarchs are generally understood: they had a regal and sacerdotal power in the order of God. In the behalf of the patriarchs God had often especially interfered: in behalf of Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.17">Gen 12:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.20.3">Gen 20:3</reference>; and of Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.24">Gen 31:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.34.26">Gen 34:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.5">Gen 35:5</reference>. But the title may be applied to all the Jewish people, who were the anointed, as they were the elect and peculiar people of God. See on <reference osisRef="Heb.11.26">Heb 11:26</reference> (note).
entries.5db763e4e064a15c830bbf48f57240371f93d289: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen13654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13655" type="x-p"/> Let the heavens be glad - "Let the supreme angels be glad, and the inhabitants of the earth rejoice." - T. In this place the Targumist uses the Greek word αγγελοι, angels, in Hebrew letters thus, אנגלי angeley.
entries.a58f4077b6c68911b7f8f850bb9fccf8e42f7fe4: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen13655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13656" type="x-p"/> Save us, O God of our salvation - As he is the saving God, so we may pray to him to save us. To pray to God under the attribute the influence of which we need, serves to inspire much confidence. I am weak; Almighty God, help me! I am ignorant; O thou Father of lights, teach me! I am lost; O merciful God, save me; etc. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.96.1-Psa.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> (note) and Psalm 105 (note).
entries.26ffe560a80ffad93149914d909629206249e192: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen13656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13657" type="x-p"/> Zadok the priest - Both Zadok and Abiathar were high priests at this time: the former David established at Gibeah, or Gibeon, where the ark had been all the days of Saul; and the latter he established at Jerusalem, where the ark now was: so there were two high priests, and two distinct services; but there was only one ark. How long the service at Gibeon was continued we cannot tell; the principal functions were no doubt performed at Jerusalem.
entries.4b6ce147e128c90c481bfa60b3c631596c9f66a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen13657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13658" type="x-p"/> Musical instruments of God - Ad canendum Deo, "to sing to God." - Vulgate. Των ωδων του Θεου, "of the sons of God." - Septuagint. The Syriac is remarkable: "These were upright men who did not sing unto God with instruments of music, nor with drums, nor with listra, nor with straight nor crooked pipes, nor with cymbals; but they sang before the Lord Almighty with a joyous mouth, and with a pure and holy prayer, and with innocence and integrity." The Arabic is nearly the same. None of the versions understand the words כלי שיר האלהים keley shir haelohim as implying instruments of music of God, but instruments employed in the song of God, or to praise God; as also the Targum. Query, Did God ever ordain instruments of music to be used in his worship? Can they be used in Christian assemblies according to the spirit of Christianity? Has Jesus Christ, or his apostles, ever commanded or sanctioned the use of them? Were they ever used any where in the apostolic Church? Does the use of them at present, in Christian congregations, ever increase the spirit of devotion? Does it ever appear that bands of musicians, either in their collective or individual capacity, are more spiritual, or as spiritual, as the other parts of the Church of Christ? Is there less pride, self-will, stubbornness, insubordination, lightness, and frivolity, among such persons, than among the other professors of Christianity found in the same religious society? Is it ever remarked or known that musicians in the house of God have attained to any depth of piety, or superior soundness of understanding, in the things of God? Is it ever found that those Churches and Christian societies which have and use instruments of music in Divine worship are more holy, or as holy, as those societies which do not use them? And is it always found that the ministers which affect and recommend them to be used in the worship of Almighty God, are the most spiritual men, and the most spiritual and useful preachers? Can mere sounds, no matter how melodious, where no word nor sentiment is or can be uttered, be considered as giving praise to God? Is it possible that pipes or strings of any kind can give God praise? Can God be pleased with sounds which are emitted by no sentient being, and have in themselves no meaning? If these questions cannot be answered in the affirmative: then, query, Is not the introduction of such instruments into the worship of God antichristian, and calculated to debase and ultimately ruin the spirit and influence of the Gospel of Jesus Christ? And should not all who wish well to the spread and establishment of pure and undefiled religion, lift up their hand, their influence, and their voice against them? The argument from their use in the Jewish service is futile in the extreme when applied to Christianity.  <chapter eID="1Chr.16"/> <div eID="gen13658" type="x-p"/>

entries.8b774e1e0d1a16f61fb989be63fc29e17b41a040: <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.1-1Chr.16.3">1Ch 16:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic">The religious festival, and the arrangement of the sacred service before the ark of the covenant in the city of David</hi>. - This section is not found in 2nd Samuel, where the Conclusion of this whole description (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.43">1Ch 16:43</reference>, Chron.) follows immediately upon the feasting of the people by the king, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.16.19">1Ch 16:19</reference></hi> and 1Ch 16:20.
entries.ed040d74b254539a91e1b9344fd54e0c66737ee1: <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.4-1Chr.16.6">1Ch 16:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen5746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5747" type="x-p"/> When the solemnity of the transfer of the ark, the sacrificial meal, and the dismissal of the people with a blessing, and a distribution of food, were ended, David set in order the service of the Levites in the holy tent on Zion. He appointed before the ark, from among the Levites, servants to praise and celebrate God, i.e., singers and players to sing psalms as a part of the regular worship. להזכּיר, literally, “in order to bring into remembrance,” is not to praise in general, but is to be interpreted according to the להזכּיר in the superscription of Ps 38 and <reference osisRef="Ps.70.1-Ps.70.5">Psa 70:1-5</reference>, by which these psalms are designated as the appointed prayers at the presentation of the Azcarah of the meat-offering (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.2">Lev 2:2</reference>). הזכּיר accordingly is a <hi type="italic">denom</hi>. from אזכּרה, to present the Azcarah (cf. Del. on <reference osisRef="Ps.38.1">Psa 38:1</reference>), and is in our verse to be understood of the recital of these prayer-songs with musical accompaniment. הודות, to confess, refers to the psalms in which invocation and acknowledgment of the name of the Lord predominates, and הלּל to those in which praise (Hallelujah) is the prominent feature. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.5">1Ch 16:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.6">1Ch 16:6</reference> there follow the names of the Levites appointed for this purpose, who have all been already mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19-1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:19-21</reference> as accompanying the ark in its transmission; but all who are there spoken of are not included in our list here. Of the chief singers only Asaph is mentioned, Heman and Ethan being omitted; of the singers and players of the second rank, only nine; six of the eight nebel-players (1Ch 15:20. יעיאל is a transcriber’s error for יעזיאל, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18">1Ch 15:18</reference>), and only three of the six kinnor-players; while instead of seven trumpet-blowing priests only two are named, viz., Benaiah, one of those seven, and Jehaziel, whose name does not occur in 1Ch 15:24.
entries.48ad3dafae742f1236a0fd18844282b6a3f1504c: <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.7">1Ch 16:7</reference> <div eID="gen5747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5748" type="x-p"/> On that day David first committed it to Asaph and his sons to give thanks to Jahve. נתן is to be connected with בּיד, which is separated from it by several words, and denotes to hand over to, here to commit to, to enjoin upon, since that which David committed to Asaph was the carrying out of a business which he enjoined, not an object which may be given into the hand. ההוּא בּיּום is accented by אז. בּראשׁ, “at the beginning,” “at first,” to bring out the fact that liturgical singing was then first introduced. אחיו, the brethren of Asaph, are the Levites appointed to the same duty, whose names are given in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.5">1Ch 16:5</reference>, 1Ch 16:6. But in order to give a more exact description of the ליהוה הודות committed to Asaph in vv. 8-36, a song of thanks and praise is given, which the Levites were to sing as part of the service with instrumental accompaniment. It is not expressly said that this song was composed by David for this purpose; but if Asaph with his singers was to perform the service committed to him, he must have been provided with the songs of praise (psalms) which were necessary for this purpose; and if David were in any way the founder of the liturgical psalmody, he, as a richly endowed psalm-singer, would doubtless compose the necessary liturgical psalms. These considerations render it very probable that the following psalm was a hymn composed by David for the liturgical song in the public worship. The psalm is as follows: -   8  Give thanks unto Jahve; preach His name; <div eID="gen5748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5749" type="x-p"/> Make known His deeds among the peoples:   9  Sing to Him, play to Him; <div eID="gen5749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5750" type="x-p"/> Meditate upon all His wondrous works. 10  Glory ye in His holy name: <div eID="gen5750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5751" type="x-p"/> Let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord. 11  Seek ye the Lord, and His strength; <div eID="gen5751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5752" type="x-p"/> Seek His face continually. 12  Remember His wonders which He has done; <div eID="gen5752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5753" type="x-p"/> His wondrous works, and the judgments of His mouth; 13  O seed of Israel, His servants, <div eID="gen5753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5754" type="x-p"/> Sons of Jacob, His chosen. 14  He, Jahve, is our God; <div eID="gen5754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5755" type="x-p"/> His judgments go forth over all the earth. 15  Remember eternally His covenant, <div eID="gen5755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5756" type="x-p"/> The word which He commanded to a thousand generations: 16  Which He made with Abraham, <div eID="gen5756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5757" type="x-p"/> And His oath to Isaac; 17  And caused it to stand to Jacob for a law, <div eID="gen5757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5758" type="x-p"/> To Israel as an everlasting covenant; 18  Saying, “To thee I give the land Canaan, <div eID="gen5758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5759" type="x-p"/> As the heritage meted out to you.” 19  When ye were still a people to be numbered, <div eID="gen5759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5760" type="x-p"/> Very few, and strangers therein, 20  And they wandered from nation to nation, <div eID="gen5760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5761" type="x-p"/> From one kingdom to another people, 21 He suffered no man to oppress them, <div eID="gen5761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5762" type="x-p"/> And reproved kings for their sake: 22  “Touch not mine anointed ones, <div eID="gen5762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5763" type="x-p"/> And do my prophets no harm.” 23  Sing unto Jahve, all the lands; <div eID="gen5763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5764" type="x-p"/> Show forth from day to day His salvation. 24  Declare His glory among the heathen, <div eID="gen5764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5765" type="x-p"/> Among all people His wondrous works. 25  For great is Jahve, and greatly to be praised; <div eID="gen5765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5766" type="x-p"/> And to be feared is He above all the gods. 26  For all the gods of the people are idols; <div eID="gen5766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5767" type="x-p"/> And Jahve has made the heavens. 27  Majesty and splendour is before Him; <div eID="gen5767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5768" type="x-p"/> Strength and joy are in His place. 28  Give unto Jahve, ye kindreds of the people, <div eID="gen5768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5769" type="x-p"/> Give unto Jahve glory and strength. 29  Give unto Jahve the honour of His name: <div eID="gen5769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5770" type="x-p"/> Bring an offering, and come before His presence; <div eID="gen5770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5771" type="x-p"/> Worship the Lord in the holy ornaments. 30  Tremble before Him, all the lands; <div eID="gen5771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5772" type="x-p"/> Then will the earth stand fast unshaking. 31  Let the heavens be glad, and the earth rejoice; <div eID="gen5772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5773" type="x-p"/> And they will say among the heathen, Jahve is King. 32  Let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof; <div eID="gen5773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5774" type="x-p"/> Let the field exult, and all that is thereon. 33  Then shall the trees of the wood rejoice <div eID="gen5774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5775" type="x-p"/> Before the Lord; for He comes to judge the earth. 34  Give thanks unto Jahve, for He is good; <div eID="gen5775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5776" type="x-p"/> For His mercy endureth for ever. 35  And say, “Save us, God of our salvation:” <div eID="gen5776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5777" type="x-p"/> And gather us together, and deliver us from the heathen, <div eID="gen5777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5778" type="x-p"/> To give thanks to Thy holy name, <div eID="gen5778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5779" type="x-p"/> To glory in Thy praise. 36  Blessed be Jahve, the God of Israel, <div eID="gen5779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5780" type="x-p"/> From everlasting to everlasting.<hi type="italic">And all the people said Amen, and praised Jahve.</hi>
entries.879a82a7c2ed2a53a82674ff4137c794bc7b92bc: <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:8-36</reference> <div eID="gen5780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5781" type="x-p"/> This hymn forms a connected and uniform whole. Beginning with a summons to praise the Lord, and to seek His face (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8-1Chr.16.11">1Ch 16:8-11</reference>), the singer exhorts his people to remember the wondrous works of the Lord (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.12-1Chr.16.14">1Ch 16:12-14</reference>), and the covenant which He made with the patriarchs to give them the land of Canaan (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.15-1Chr.16.18">1Ch 16:15-18</reference>), and confirms his exhortation by pointing out how the Lord, in fulfilment of His promise, had mightily and gloriously defended the patriarchs (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.19-1Chr.16.22">1Ch 16:19-22</reference>). But all the world also are to praise Him as the only true and almighty God (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23-1Chr.16.27">1Ch 16:23-27</reference>), and all peoples do homage to Him with sacrificial gifts (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.28-1Chr.16.30">1Ch 16:28-30</reference>); and that His kingdom may be acknowledged among the heathen, even inanimate nature will rejoice at His coming to judgment (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.31-1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:31-33</reference>). In conclusion, we have again the summons to thankfulness,combined with a prayer that God would further vouchsafe salvation; and a doxology rounds off the whole (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:34-36</reference>). When we consider the contents of the whole hymn, it is manifest that it contains nothing which would be at all inconsistent with the belief that it was composed by David for the above-mentioned religious service. There is nowhere any reference to the condition of the people in exile, nor yet to the circumstances after the exile. The subject of the praise to which Israel is summoned is the covenant which God made with Abraham, and the wonderful way in which the patriarchs were led. The summons to the heathen to acknowledge Jahve as alone God and King of the world, and to come before His presence with sacrificial offerings, together with the thought that Jahve will come to judge the earth, belong to the Messianic hopes. These had formed themselves upon the foundation of the promises given to the patriarchs, and the view they had of Jahve as Judge of the heathen, when He led His people out of Egypt,so early, that even in the song of Moses at the Red Sea (Ex. 15), and the song of the pious Hannah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1-1Sam.2.10">1Sa 2:1-10</reference>), we meet with the first germs of them; and what we find in David and the prophets after him are only further development of these. <div eID="gen5781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5782" type="x-p"/> Yet all the later commentators, with the exception of Hitzig,<hi type="italic">die Psalmen</hi>, ii. S. ix.f., judge otherwise as to the origin of this festal hymn. Because the first half of it (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8-1Chr.16.22">1Ch 16:8-22</reference>) recurs in <reference osisRef="Ps.105.1-Ps.105.15">Psa 105:1-15</reference>, the second (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23-1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:23-33</reference>) in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference>, and the conclusion (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:34-36</reference>) in Ps.Psa 106:1, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47-Ps.106.48">Psa 106:47-48</reference>, it is concluded that the author of the Chronicle compounded the hymn from these three psalms, in order to reproduce the festive songs which were heard after the ark had been brought in, in the same free way in which the speeches in Thucydides and Livy reproduce what was spoken at various times. Besides the later commentators, Aug. Koehler (in the <hi type="italic">Luth. Ztschr.</hi> 1867, S. 289ff.) and C. Ehrt (<hi type="italic">Abfassungszeit und Abschluss des Psalters</hi>, Leipz. 1869, S. 41ff.) are of the same opinion. The possibility that our hymn may have arisen in this way cannot be denied; for such a supposition would be in so far consistent with the character of the Chronicle, as we find in it speeches which have not been reported <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> by the hearers, but are given in substance or in freer outline by the author of our Chronicle, or, as is more probable, by the author of the original documents made use of by the chronicler. But this view can only be shown to be correct if it corresponds to the relation in which our hymn may be ascertained to stand to the three psalms just mentioned. Besides the face that its different sections are again met with scattered about in different psalms, the grounds for supposing that our hymn is not an original poem are mainly the want of connection in the transition from <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.22">1Ch 16:22</reference> to v.23, and from <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:33</reference> to v.34; the fact that in v.35 we have a verse referring to the Babylonian exile borrowed from Ps 106; ; and that <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:36</reference> is even the doxology of the fourth book of Psalms, taken to be a component part of the psalm. These two latter grounds would be decisive, if the facts on which they rest were well authenticated. If. <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:36</reference> really contained only the doxology of the fourth book of Psalms-which, like the doxologies of the first, second, and third books (Ps. 41:14; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.18-Ps.72.19">Psa 72:18-19</reference>, and 89:53), was merely formally connected with the psalm, without being a component part of it-there could be no doubt that the author of the Chronicle had taken the conclusion of his hymn from our collection of psalms, as these doxologies only date from the originators of our collection. But this is not the state of the case. <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference> does, it is true, occupy in our Psalter the place of the doxology to the fourth book, but belonged, as Bertheau also acknowledges, originally to the psalm itself. For not only is it different in form from the doxologies of the first three books, not having the double ואמן אמן with which these books close, but it concludes with the simple הללוּ־יהּ אמן. If the ואמן אמן connected by ו is, in the Old Testament language, exclusively confined to these doxologies, which thus approach the language of the liturgical Beracha of the second temple, as Del. <hi type="italic">Ps</hi>. p. 15 rightly remarks, while in Num 5:22 and <reference osisRef="Neh.8.6">Neh 8:6</reference> only אמן אמן without copulative w occurs, it is just this peculiarity of the liturgical Beracha which is wanting, both in the concluding verse of the 106th Psalm and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:36</reference> of our festal hymn. Moreover, the remainder of the verse in question - the last clause of it, “And let all the people say Amen, Halleluiah,” - does not suit the hypothesis that the verse is the doxology appended to the conclusion of the fourth book by the collector of the Psalms, since, as <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi> in his commentary on the psalm rightly remarks, “it is inconceivable that the people should join in that which, as mere closing doxology of a book, would have no religious character;” and “the praise in the conclusion of the psalm beautifully coincides with its commencement, and the Halleluiah of the end is shown to be an original part of the psalm by its correspondence with the beginning.”<note placement="foot">Bertheau also rightly says: “If in Ps 72 (as also in Ps 89 and 91) the author of the doxology himself says Amen, while in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference> the saying of the Amen is committed to the people, this difference can only arise from the face that Ps 106 originally concluded with the exhortation to say Amen.” Hitzig speaks with still more decision, <hi type="italic">die Pss.</hi> (1865), ii. S. x.: “If (in Ps 106) <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference> is the conclusion, a proper ending is wanting; while <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference>, on the contrary, places the psalm on a level with Ps 103-105; 107. Who can believe that the author himself, for the purpose of ending the fourth book with <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference>, caused the psalm to extend to the <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference>? In the Chronicle, the people whom the verse mentions are present from 1 Chron 15:3-16:2, while in the psalm no one can see how they should come in there. Whether the verse belong to the psalm or not, the turning to all the people, and the causing the people to say Amen, Amen, instead of the writer, has no parallel in the Psalms, and is explicable only on the supposition that it comes from the Chronicle. Afterwards a Diaskeuast might be satisfied to take the verse as the boundary-stone of a book.”</note> <div eID="gen5782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5783" type="x-p"/> The last verse of our hymn does not therefore presuppose the existence of the collection of psalms, nor in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.35">1Ch 16:35</reference> is there any indubitable reference to the exilic time. The words, “Say, 'Save us, Thou God of our salvation; gather us together, and deliver us from among the heathen,' “ do not presuppose that the people had been previously led away into the Chaldean exile, but only the dispersion of prisoners of war, led away captive into an enemy’s land after a defeat. This usually occurred after each defeat of Israel by their enemies, and it was just such cases Solomon had in view in his prayer, 1Ki 8:46-50. <div eID="gen5783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5784" type="x-p"/> The decision as to the origin of this festal hymn, therefore, depends upon its internal characteristics, and the result of a comparison of the respective texts. The song in itself forms, as Hitz. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi> S. 19 rightly judges, “a thoroughly coherent and organic whole. The worshippers of Jahve are to sing His praise in memory of His covenant which He made with their fathers, and because of which He protected them (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.18-1Chr.16.22">1Ch 16:18-22</reference>). But all the world also are to praise Him, the only true God (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23-1Chr.16.27">1Ch 16:23-27</reference>); the peoples are to come before Him with gifts; yea, even inanimate nature is to pay the King and Judge its homage (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.28-1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:28-33</reference>). Israel - and with this the end returns to the beginning-is to thank Jahve, and invoke His help against the heathen (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34">1Ch 16:34</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.35">1Ch 16:35</reference>).” This exposition of the symmetrical disposition of the psalm is not rendered questionable by the objections raised by Koehler,<hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>; nor can the recurrence of the individual parts of it in three different psalms of itself at all prove that in the Chronicle we have not the original form of the hymn. “There is nothing to hinder us from supposing that the author of <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> may be the same as the author of Ps 105 and 106; but even another might be induced by example to appropriate the first half of 1Ch 16:8., as his predecessor had appropriated the second, and it would naturally occur to him to supply from his own resources the continuation which had been already taken away and made use of” (Hitz. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>). A similar phenomenon is the recurrence of the second half of Psa 40:17. as an independent psalm, <reference osisRef="Ps.70.1">Psa 70:1</reference>-5. “But it is also readily seen,”continues Hitzig, “how easily the psalmist might separate the last three verses from each other (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:34-36</reference> of the Chronicle), and set them as a frame round Ps 106. <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34">1Ch 16:34</reference> is not less suitable in the Chronicle for the commencement of a paragraph than in Ps 107, which <reference osisRef="Ps.107.6">Psa 107:6</reference> would admit of no continuation, but was the proper end. On the other hand, we can scarcely believe that the chronicler compiled his song first from Ps 105, then from <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference>, and lastly from Ps 106, striking off from this latter only the beginning and the end.” <div eID="gen5784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5785" type="x-p"/> Finally, if we compare the text of our hymn with the text of these psalms, the divergences are of such a sort that we cannot decide with certainty which of the two texts is the original. To pass over such critically indifferent variations as פּיהוּ, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.12">1Ch 16:12</reference>, for פּיו, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.5">Psa 105:5</reference>; the omission of the <hi type="italic">nota acc.</hi> את, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.18">1Ch 16:18</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Ps.105.10">Psa 105:10</reference>, and vice versa in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.3">Psa 96:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.24">1Ch 16:24</reference>; היּער עצי, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:33</reference>, instead of היּער כּל־עצי, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.12">Psa 96:12</reference>, - the chronicler has in יצחק, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.16">1Ch 16:16</reference>, instead of ישׂחק, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.9">Psa 105:9</reference>, and יעלץ, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.32">1Ch 16:32</reference>, instead of יעלז, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.12">Psa 96:12</reference>, the earlier and more primitive form; in תּרעוּ אל בּנביאי, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.22">1Ch 16:22</reference>, instead of תּרעוּ אל לנביאי, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.15">Psa 105:15</reference>, a quite unusual construction; and in יום אל מיּום, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23">1Ch 16:23</reference>, the older form (cf. Num 30:15), instead of ליום מיּום, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.2">Psa 96:2</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Esth.3.7">Est 3:7</reference>; while, on the other hand, instead of the unexampled phrase לעשׁקם אדם הנּיח, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.14">Psa 105:14</reference>, there stands in the Chronicle the usual phrase לאישׁ הנּיח, and שׂדי dna , in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.12">Psa 96:12</reference> is the poetical form for the השּׂדה of 1Ch 16:32. More important are the wider divergences: not so much ישׂראל זרע, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.13">1Ch 16:13</reference>, for אברהם זרע, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.6">Psa 105:6</reference>, in which latter case it is doubtful whether the עבדּו refers to the patriarchs or to the people, and consequently, as the <hi type="italic">parallelismus membrorum</hi> demands the latter references, ישׂראל is clearly the more correct and intelligible; but rather than the others, viz., זכרוּ, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.15">1Ch 16:15</reference>, for זכר, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.8">Psa 105:8</reference>; since זכרוּ not only corresponds to the זכרוּ of <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.11">1Ch 16:11</reference>, but alto to the use made of the song for the purposes stated in the Chronicle; while, on the contrary, זכר of the psalm corresponds to the object of the psalm, viz., to exalt the covenant grace shown to the patriarchs. Connected with this also is the reading בּהיותכם, “when ye (sons of Jacob) were” (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.19">1Ch 16:19</reference>), instead of בּהיותם, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.12">Psa 105:12</reference>, “when they (the patriarchs) were,” since the narrative of what the Lord had done demanded בהיותם. Now the more likely the reference of the words to the patriarchs was to suggest itself, the more unlikely is the hypothesis of an alteration into בהיותכם; and the text of the Chronicle being the more difficult, is consequently to be regarded as the earlier. Moreover, the divergences of <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23">1Ch 16:23</reference> to 33 of our hymn from <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> are such as would result from its having been prepared for the above-mentioned solemn festival. The omission of the two strophes, “Sing unto Jahve a new song, sing unto Jahve, bless His name” (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.96.2">Psa 96:2</reference></hi>), in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.23">1Ch 16:23</reference> of the Chronicle might be accounted for by regarding that part of our hymn as an abridgment by the chronicler of the original song, when connecting it with the preceding praise of God, were it certain on other grounds that <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> was the original; but if the chronicler’s hymn be the original, we may just as well believe that this section was amplified when it was made into an independent psalm. A comparison of <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:33</reference> (Chron.) with the end of the 96th Psalm favours this last hypothesis, for in the Chronicle the repetition of בּא כּי is wanting, as well as the second hemistich of Psa 96:13. The whole of the 13th verse recurs, with a single בּא כּי, at the end of the 98th Psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.98.9">Psa 98:9</reference>), and the thought is borrowed from the Davidic Psa 9:9. The strophes in the beginning of <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference>, which are omitted from <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.16">1Ch 16:16</reference>, often recur. The phrase, “Sing unto Jahve a new song,” is met within <reference osisRef="Ps.33.3">Psa 33:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Psa 98:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.149.1">Psa 149:1</reference>, and חדשׁ שׁיר in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference>, a Davidic psalm. את־שׁמו בּרכוּ is also met with in <reference osisRef="Ps.100.4">Psa 100:4</reference>; and still more frequently את־יהוה בּרכוּ, in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.2">Psa 103:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.22">Psa 103:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.134.1">Psa 134:1</reference>, and elsewhere, even as early as Deborah’s song, Jdg 5:2, Jdg 5:9; while ליהוה שׁירוּ occurs in the song of Moses, Exo 15:1. Since, then, the strophes of the 96th Psalm are only reminiscences of, and phrases which we find in, the oldest religious songs of the Israelites, it is clear that <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> is not an original poem. It is rather the re-grouping of the well-known and current thoughts; and the fact that it is so, favours the belief that all which this psalm contains at the beginning and end, which the Chronicle does not contain, is merely an addition made by the poet who transformed this part of the chronicler’s hymn into an independent psalm for liturgical purposes. This purpose clearly appears in such variations as בּמקדּשׁו ותפארת, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.6">Psa 96:6</reference>, instead of בּמקמו וחדוה, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.27">1Ch 16:27</reference>, and לחצרותיו וּבאוּ, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.8">Psa 96:8</reference>, instead of לפניו וּבאוּ, 1Ch 16:29. Neither the word מקדּשׁ nor the mention of “courts” is suitable in a hymn sung at the consecration of the holy tent in Zion, for at that time the old national sanctuary with the altar in the court (the tabernacle) still stood in Gibeon. <div eID="gen5785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5786" type="x-p"/> Here, therefore, the text of the Chronicle corresponds to the circumstances of David’s time, while the mention of מקדּשׁ and of courts in the psalm presupposes the existence of the temple with its courts as the sanctuary of the people of Israel. Now a post-exilic poet would scarcely have paid so much attention to this delicate distinction between times and circumstances as to alter, in the already existing psalms, out of which he compounded this festal hymn, the expressions which were not suitable to the Davidic time. Against this, the use of the unusual word חדוה drow lau, joy, which occurs elsewhere only in <reference osisRef="Neh.10.8">Neh 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.10.10">Neh 10:10</reference>, and in Chaldee in Ezr 6:18, is no valid objection, for the use of the verb חדה as early as <reference osisRef="Exod.18.9">Exo 18:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.3.6">Job 3:6</reference> shows that the word does not belong to the later Hebrew. The discrepancy also between <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.30">1Ch 16:30</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.31">1Ch 16:31</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.96.9-Ps.96.11">Psa 96:9-11</reference>, namely, the omission in the Chronicle of the strophe בּמישׁרים עמּים ידין (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">Psa 96:10</reference>), and the placing of the clause מלך יהוה בגּוים      ויאמרוּ after הארץ ותגל (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.31">1Ch 16:31</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.96.10">Psa 96:10</reference>), does not really prove anything as to the priority of <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference>-13. Hitzig, indeed, thinks that since by the omission of the one member the parallelism of the verses is disturbed, and a triple verse appears where all the others are double merely, and because by this alteration the clause,”Say among the people, Jahve is King,” has come into an apparently unsuitable position, between an exhortation to the heaven and earth to rejoice, and the roaring of the sea and its fulness, this clause must have been unsuitably placed by a copyist’s error. But the transposition cannot be so explained; for not only is that one member of the verse misplaced, but also the אמרוּ of the psalm is altered into ויאמרוּ, and moreover, we get no explanation of the omission of the strophe וגו ידין. If we consider ויאמרוּ (with ו consecutive), “then will they say,” we see clearly that it corresponds to וגו ירנּנוּ אז in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:33</reference>; and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.30">1Ch 16:30</reference> the recognition of Jahve’s kingship over the peoples is represented as the issue and effect of the joyful exultation of the heaven and earth, just as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.32">1Ch 16:32</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:33</reference> the joyful shouting of the trees of the field before Jahve as He comes to judge the earth, is regarded as the result of the roaring of the sea and the gladness of the fields. The אמרוּ of the psalm, on the other hand, the summons to the Israelites to proclaim that Jahve is King among the peoples, is, after the call, “Let the whole earth tremble before Him,” a somewhat tame expression; and after it, again, we should not expect the much stronger וגו תּכּון אף. When we further consider that the clause which follows in the Chronicle, “He will judge the people in uprightness,” is a reminiscence of <reference osisRef="Ps.9.9">Psa 9:9</reference>, we must hold the text of the Chronicle to be here also the original, and the divergences in <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> for alterations, which were occasioned by the changing of a part of our hymn into an independent psalm. Finally, there can be no doubt as to the priority of the chronicler’s hymn in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34">1Ch 16:34</reference>-36. The author of the Chronicle did not require to borrow the liturgical formula וגו טוב כּי ליהוה הודוּ from <reference osisRef="Ps.106.1">Psa 106:1</reference>, for it occurs in as complete a form in <reference osisRef="Ps.97.1">Psa 97:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.1">Psa 118:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.29">Psa 118:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.136.1">Psa 136:1</reference>, and, not to mention <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.13">2Ch 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.3">2Ch 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2Ch 20:21</reference>, is a current phrase with Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.11">Jer 33:11</reference>), and is without doubt an ancient liturgical form. <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.35">1Ch 16:35</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:36</reference>, too, contain such divergences from <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference>, that it is in the highest degree improbable that they were borrowed from that psalm. Not only is the prayer וגו הושׁיענוּ introduced by אמרוּ, but also, instead of אלהינוּ יהוה of the psalm, we have ישׁענוּ אלהי; and to וקבּצנוּ, והצּילנוּ is added, - a change which causes the words to lose the reference to the Chaldean exile contained in the text of the Psalms. The post-exilic author of the Chronicle would scarcely have obliterated this reference, and certainly would not have done so in such a delicate fashion, had he taken the verse from Ps 106. A much more probable supposition is, that the post-exilic author of the 106th Psalm appropriated the concluding verse of David’s to him well-known hymn, and modified it to make it fit into his poem. Indubitable instances of such alterations are to be found in the conclusion, where the statement of the chronicler, that all the people said Amen and praised Jahve, is made to conform to the psalm, beginning as it does with Halleluiah, by altering ויּאמרוּ into ואמר, “and let them say,” and of ליהוה והלּל into הללוּ־יהּ. <div eID="gen5786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5787" type="x-p"/> On the whole, therefore, we must regard the opinion that David composed our psalm for the above-mentioned festival as by far the most probable. The psalm itself needs no further commentary; but compare Delitzsch on the parallel psalms and parts of psalms.<hi type="italic">Division of the Levites for the management of the public worship</hi>. - At the same time as he set up the ark in the tent erected for it on Mount Zion, David had prepared a new locality for the public worship. The Mosaic tabernacle had continued, with its altar of burnt-offering, to be the general place of worship for the congregation of Israel even during the long period when the ark was separated from it, and it was even yet to be so; and it became necessary, in order to carry on the religious service in both of these sanctuaries, to divide the staff of religious officials: and this David now undertook.
entries.16e347e33da15a806d97346234adee863800300f: <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.37-1Chr.16.38">1Ch 16:37-38</reference> <div eID="gen5787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5788" type="x-p"/> Before the ark he left Asaph with his brethren (ל( nerht before the <hi type="italic">accus. obj.</hi>, according to the later usage), to serve, to minister there continually. בּיומו לדבר־יום, “according to the matter of the day on its day,” i.e., according to the service necessary for each day; cf. for this expression, <reference osisRef="Exod.5.13">Exo 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.5.19">Exo 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.16.4">Exo 16:4</reference>, etc. “And Obed-edom and their brethren.” In these words there is a textual error: the plural suffix in אחיהם shows that after אדום עבד at least one name has been dropped out. But besides that, the relation in which the words, “and Obed-edom the son of Jeduthun, and Hosah, to be porters,” stand to the preceding clause, “and Obed-edom and their brethren,” is obscure. Against the somewhat general idea, that the words are to be taken in an explicative sense, “and Obed-edom indeed,” etc., the objection suggests itself, that Obed-edom is here defined to be the son of Jeduthun, and would seem to be thereby distinguished from the preceding Obed-edom. In addition to that, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:21</reference> and Obed-edom is mentioned among the singers, and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.24">1Ch 16:24</reference> one of the doorkeepers bears that name, and they are clearly distinguished as being different persons. On the other hand, however, the identity of the two Obed-edoms in our verse is supported by the fact that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.4-1Chr.26.8">1Ch 26:4-8</reference> the doorkeepers Obed-edom with his sons and brethren number sixty-two, which comes pretty nearly up to the number mentioned in our verse, viz., sixty-eight. Yet we cannot regard this circumstance as sufficient to identify the two, and must leave the question undecided, because the text of our verse is defective. Jeduthun the father of Obed-edom is different from the chief musician Jeduthun (= Ethan); for the chief musician is a descendant of Merari, while the doorkeeper Jeduthun belongs to the Korahites (i.e., Kohathites): see on 1Ch 26:4.
entries.998b5aa609c7b65f43a94df443baf1ccdbf37ad8: <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39-1Chr.16.40">1Ch 16:39-40</reference> צדוק ואת is still dependent on the ויּעזב in 1Ch 16:37. The priest Zadok with his brethren he left before the tent of Jahve, i.e., the tabernacle at the Bamah in Gibeon. For בּמה see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.13">2Ch 1:13</reference>, and for Zadok on 2Ch 6:12. It is surprising here that no priest is named as superintendent or overseer of the sacrificial worship in the tent of the ark of the covenant. But the omission is accounted for by the fact that our chapter treats properly only of the arrangement of the sacred music connected with the worship, and Zadok is mentioned as overseer of the sanctuary of the tabernacle at Gibeon only in order to introduce the statement as to the Levitic singers and players assigned to that sanctuary. Without doubt Abiathar as high priest had the oversight of the sacrificial worship in the sanctuary of the tabernacle: see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.16">1Ch 18:16</reference>; with <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.40">1Ch 16:40</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38">Exo 29:38</reference>; Num 28:3, Num 28:6. לכל־הכּתוּב corresponds to להעלות: and in reference to all, i.e., to look after all, which was written. This refers not only to the bringing of the sacrifices prescribed, in addition to the daily burnt-offering, but in general to everything that it was the priests’ duty to do in the sanctuary.
entries.dec6b6a29e22607573c374bfa02ad41b51aa92cb: <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.41-1Chr.16.42">1Ch 16:41-42</reference> ועמּהם, and with them (with Zadok and his brethren) were Heman and Jeduthun, i.e., (the two other chief musicians, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1Ch 15:19</reference>), with the other chosen famous, sc. singers (בשׁמות נקּבוּ, see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.31">1Ch 12:31</reference>). To these belonged those of the number named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.18-1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:18-21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.24">1Ch 15:24</reference>, who are not mentioned among those assigned to Asaph in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.5">1Ch 16:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.6">1Ch 16:6</reference>, and probably also a number of others whose names have not been handed down. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.42">1Ch 16:42</reference>, if the text be correct, וידוּתוּן הימן can only be in apposition to עמּהם: “and with them, viz., with Heman and Jeduthun, were trumpets,” etc. But, not to mention the difficulty that passages analogous and parallel to this statement are not to be found, the mention of these two chief musicians in the connection is surprising; for the musical instruments mentioned are not merely the מצלתּים (s. <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1Ch 15:19</reference>) played by them, but also the חצצרות which the priests blew, and other instruments. Moreover, the names Heman and Jeduthun are not found here in the lxx, and have probably been inserted in our verse by some copyist from <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.41">1Ch 16:41</reference>, which likewise begins with ועמּהם. If we omit these names, then, the verse contains no other difficulty worthy of consideration, or any which would occasion or necessitate such violent alterations of the text as Berth. has proposed. The suffix in עמּהם refers to the persons mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.41">1Ch 16:41</reference>, Heman, Jeduthun, and the other chosen ones. “With them were,” i.e., they had by them, trumpets, cymbals, etc. The ל before משׁמיעים is strange, since משׁמיעים is in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.16">1Ch 15:16</reference> connected with מצלתּים as an adjective, and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1Ch 15:19</reference> we have להשׁמיע. But if we compare <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.5">1Ch 16:5</reference> of our chapter, where משׁמיע is predicate to Asaph, “Asaph gave forth clear notes with cymbals,” then here also למשׁמיעים in connection with מצלתּים is thoroughly justified in the signification, “and cymbals for those who gave forth the notes or the melody,” i.e., for Heman and Jeduthun. הא שׁיר כּלי are the other instruments used in the service of the song, viz., the <hi type="italic">nablia</hi> and <hi type="italic">kinnoroth</hi>. “The sons of Jeduthun for the gate,” i.e., as doorkeepers. As Obed-edom, who was doorkeeper by the ark, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.38">1Ch 16:38</reference>, was likewise a son of Jeduthun, here other sons of the same Jeduthun, brothers of Obed-edom, must be meant, the number of whom, if we may judge from <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.8">1Ch 26:8</reference>, was very considerable; so that the members of this family were able to attend to the doorkeeping both by the ark and in the tabernacle at Gibeon.
entries.39c0dbfd05b72b8b2222143be921b2d7b7ecc852: <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.43">1Ch 16:43</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.43">1Ch 16:43</reference> brings the account of the transfer of the ark to a conclusion, and coincides in substance with <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.19">2Sa 6:19</reference> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.6.20">2Sa 6:20</reference></hi>, where, however, there follows in addition a narrative of the scene which David had with his wife Michal. This, as <hi type="italic">res domestica</hi>, the author of the Chronicle has omitted, since the reference to it in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.29">1Ch 15:29</reference> seemed sufficient for the design of his work. לברך is not to greet, but to bless his house, just as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.2">1Ch 16:2</reference> he had already pronounced a blessing on his people in the name of God.  <chapter eID="1Chr.16"/> <div eID="gen5788" type="x-p"/>
